source: Now. Please, milady. I have some sudden unforeseen business to attend to, which involves keeping my head firmly attached to my body.
Irma, I feel I can confide in you: King Hamlet's death was no accident. I know the truth.
What can you mean? And hush your voice!
I witnessed him confessing. He was praying. He said he'd poisoned his brother.
Oh, my lady.
Do you know how many bloody secrets these walls have heard?
I don't doubt what you say is true. Mein Gott, the very servants believe it to be true.
And didn't you find the very poison he used to do it?
Indeed. Now that I am its owner, he shan't ever use it again!
Yes, perhaps it will come in handy for some little thing in the future. But if there's one thing I know for certain, it is this...
He's even got the instrument of murder in his room.
You say this, but I found no such thing! You sent me on such a wild chase, for naught!
We shall see about that, won't we? But unless that tree bears fruit, there is only one thing I know for certain.
You shall never, ever prove Claudius's guilt.
You're wrong. I know there's a way to prove this.
Then I shall have no part in it, lady.
Marcellus, I don't believe King Hamlet's death was an accident. I think he was murdered.
Hmm. Yeh soun' just like that crazy ghost!
Oh, sure. We saw th'spirit o' King Hamlet up on the walls, all angry-like. It spoke to us. Wanted vengeance. The usual.
But, neh. I don' believe it.
You spoke to King Hamlet's spirit, but this is too far-fetched?
Sure. If I don' believe you, I get ta' keep my job an' my conscience.
An' the only person that ghost seems interested in hauntin' is Hamlet!
I know for certain that King Claudius murdered his brother, Hamlet's father.
Now, Ophelia. What good can come of trading in rumors of that sort?
He might be brought to justice. He might be contained.
To whom is he an immediate danger now?
W-well, no one at the present moment, but...
Then you aim to save no one, and only destroy the lives of those who work and live under Claudius.
Look, Ophelia. Guilda and I often gallivant from place to place.
We have just one rule: Don't get involved. If you get involved with people, you only shoulder their burdens.
Suffice to say, we cannot shoulder this one.
Guildenstern, surely you'll believe me. King Claudius is a murderer. I saw him confess.
Oh, we know!
We simply don't care.
It isn't our business what becomes of this place. We're only visiting, after all!
But those beady little eyes of his -- who knows what horrors he's capable of!
What if he were to come for you, or someone you cared about? What then?
Well, it's rather difficult to kill me if he thinks I'm already dead, right?
That's why this plan is so infallible!
Oh, Ophelia. Mon dieu. I've just been struck by genius.
What if I pretended to be dead, just to see what would happen?
(Oh no. Here we go again.)
Er... I don't follow.
I've always wanted to know what my funeral would be like. Now's my chance! It's brilliant!
Ophelia, you've got to tell everyone I'm dead.
They'll all come to the graveyard for a magnificent funeral, and then... I'll jump out and surprise them.
If you do that, we'll have a wonderfully funny time pranking the others, I just know it!
And... when they find out you're alive and well after all?
Right! I'm sure they'll all be so relieved, they'll instantly forgive me!
Although, now that I think about it, with everything that's happened, this is no time for pranks.
Maybe if things were a little quieter!
Some other time, perhaps.
All right, Ophelia. Go spread the word. Tell everyone there's to be a funeral. I'll be waiting!
In the meantime, as soon as I'm able to, I'll go run and hide so as not to spoil the fun.
I've got to say hello to Hamlet first, though. It would be just rude to hide before that.
This can't possibly end well.
Horatio, I need to confide in you.
I knew Hamlet was going to kill Father.
I had this dream recently. In it, Father died by Hamlet's hand.
But it was more than a dream. It was like a vision. It felt so real.
Ophelia... it's natural to search one's memory for warning signs in the aftermath of a horrible tragedy.
But none of us can change what has come before. Only where we might go from here.
I urge you not to dwell too long in the halls of memory. Nothing good happens there.
My father will be murdered, and Hamlet will be his killer.
That I can't believe.
Hamlet... isn't in his right mind. But I'm certain, however pitifully, that that wouldn't come to pass.
How can you be so sure?
Because you, as I do, know his heart. He is an odd man, but he is not a murderer.
Well, he is now.
Hamlet, I need to speak with you.
I know you took my father's life.
Let me assure you that if you have any intention of turning the blame elsewhere, know this: I place every bit of fault with you.
You're right to do so.
This may mean nothing to you right now. Perhaps it never will. But I did not intend to kill him, Ophelia.
I mistook him for my uncle. In the moment I saw your father's face... I knew what I'd done.
I know I can never seek your forgiveness. Not after all I've done.
But perhaps someday, I can pay off some small amount of the sin I've committed.
Right now, that's all I can hope for.
You can start by revealing the location of my father's body to Bernardo.
I showed the very location to his men not long after he spoke with you. My mother-- was in shock. I couldn't leave him there with her.
It was never my intention to keep him from you. But I hope you need never look upon his state.
As I understand it, I am likely to soon leave Denmark forever.
May I go, and trouble you no more, and never give you cause to think of me again.
Do you bear my father any murderous intent? Or any intent to visit your mother's chambers?
If so, I implore you to—
I find your father an insufferable, intractable, insipid sod. But I bear him no ill will.
After all, he was steadfastly faithful to my father all his life.
And I'm certain I shall visit my mother soon, though I loathe to look at her all the same.
And, no. Now that mother's gone, I've no intent to visit her chambers ever again.
(Then if Hamlet didn't kill my father intentionally, it must have been an accident.)
(If I could only get inside the Queen's chambers and witness the awful deed myself...)
Don't meet your mother alone. Nothing good can come of it.
And it will mean my father's demise. I implore you, Hamlet. Please.
I don't understand. Why would I? Ophelia, are you... well?
Ophelia, there is only one person whose bloody death I desire, and it isn't your father, or my mother.
Ophelia, there is only one person whose bloody death I desire, and it isn't your father. Nor was it my mother.
If anything, my aim is to be slow and thorough in exposing my enemies.
Peter Quince the playwright has helped with just this matter. Together we planned something incredible.
Yes... very soon you'll see the fruits of our extensive labor.
Father... I know how this sounds, but please believe me.
Hamlet made an attempt on your life, didn't he? I knew it was going to come.
Hush. Hush, Ophelia.
Better to not discuss what took place. It was an embarrassing situation for all involved, to say the least.
No gain can come of spreading around what happened. What ought I to do, pursue action against Hamlet? I would never.
I'm alive, my darling. Suffice to say, that's all that matters.
Hamlet is going to make an attempt on your life.
Hamlet? For what purpose? No...
I-is it the King's wish?
I don't think so. I don't know, exactly. I believe Hamlet is the only man you need fear.
Does he think me an obstacle to ascending the throne, with his uncle gone?
I don't think so. I don't know, exactly.
Does this mean you believe me? And you'll stay away from him...?
Well... you know it makes me ill when you say strange things like this.
It's on my mind at the very least. Now please, don't go spreading odd portents of doom to anyone else.
(So he's believed my warning—at least a little.)
(Perhaps that's enough to keep him alive this time.)
Your Highness, we need to discuss Hamlet once more.
Oh, Ophelia. I'd meant to come find you. I didn't know what to say.
Yes, my lady. I just need to understand. What happened?
I... I couldn't save him. I wanted to. It all moved so quickly.
Many a late evening has kept me staring at my ceiling, thinking about what might happen if my son were to ever act in violence.
But when the moment came, I was rooted to the floor in fear.
My late husband Hamlet considered your father to be his greatest, most trusted friend in the world.
On our wedding night, he told me that I could always run to your father, should I need help in a dire time.
And-- he was right.
I wish I knew more than you did. I'm sorry. We simply don't have the answers, yet.
My late husband considered your father to be his greatest, most trusted friend in the world.
I cannot imagine the depth and horror of what you're feeling right now. Of what Laertes will feel.
Now it is my duty, as protector of my country, to do what I must to ensure my son never hurts any Dane again.
My lady, I know how this sounds, but I believe Hamlet is going to kill my father—in your chambers. Can you help?
That's a poor jest. And cruel of you to say.
Certainly my son is disturbed, but to call him a murderer is an insult I thought you incapable of.
Do you have any plans to meet with my father and Hamlet?
Not the both of them at once, no. What brings you such concern?
If you're worried of any misdeeds taking place in my chambers—I keep them very private. Hardly anyone has access without my explicit permission.
This is, of course, to prevent exactly that sort of sordid business from happening in the first place!
My lord, I come to you about my father.
What will you do now that Hamlet has taken his life?
The thought of such a tragedy had never crossed my mind before this.
As sovereign who swore to protect the lives of your father and all citizens, Ophelia, my sorrow is deep.
